On a headland, erosion will exploit any weakness, creating at first a cave [1]. Once the
cave reaches both sides of the headland, an arch is formed [1]. A collapse of the top of the
arch forms a stack [1].
[Max 3 marks]

Mangroves are largely located along tropical coastlines [1], although they can extend
as far north as South Korea and as far south as the southern tip of Australia [1]. They
are located in tidal estuaries [1] and in areas of muddy waters that are rich with
nutrients [1].
[Max 3 marks]

Mangroves are salt tolerant, so they can exist in tidal estuaries and coastal zones [1].
Tidal estuaries are rich in nutrients from decaying wood and leaves, so provide a
source of nutrients for the mangroves [1].
[Max 2 marks]

Mangroves are a rich source of food [1], fuel [1], building materials [1] and medicines
[1]. They help reduce wind speeds during tropical cyclones [1]. They act as natural
filters, absorbing nutrients from farming and sewage disposal [1]. There should be a
named example of a coastal area that provides examples of the importance of
mangroves.
[Max 3 marks]

Many mangroves have been destroyed to make way for food production [1],
especially rice paddies and shrimp farms [1].
[Max 2 marks]

There are many opportunities resulting from living in coastal areas, including employment in
the tourism and recreation, fishing and port industries. Many people feel ‘at home’ in coastal
areas and derive health benefits and/or other environmental services (benefits) from the area
[1]. Coastal areas also have milder climates than inland areas. Hazards in coastal areas include
storms, erosion and rising sea levels. Coastal erosion may cause some buildings to be
destroyed. Property prices can be quite high as many coastal areas attract retired and/or
wealthy residents. Most developed answers are likely to have named and located supporting
examples. Both opportunities and hazards should be stated –if only one of these categories is
stated, do not award more than 5 marks.
[Max 7 marks]
